scope: Named foreign shareholders (≥1%) of five NIFTY 50 / large-cap constituents assigned as batch 2 (Bajaj Auto, Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finserv, Bharat Electronics, Cipla), from primary SEBI Reg. 31(1)(b) shareholding-pattern filings where reachable. Only Cipla's primary filing was successfully opened and read in this pass (quarter ended 30.09.2025, pulled from cipla.com's own PDF mirror of the BSE XBRL render). The other four companies' primary sources could not be opened within the 8-fetch-per-company budget for structural reasons specific to each site (recorded in voids, not worked around): Bajaj Finance's and Bajaj Finserv's investor-relations pages (aboutbajajfinserv.com) are client-side-rendered Next.js applications that return only an empty shell to a non-browser fetch, and the one concrete document link found for Bajaj Finserv (a 'shareholding-pattern/31-march.xlsm' download) turned out to be a blank disclosure *template* dated 31-03-2016, not a filled current filing; Bajaj Auto's legacy static IR page (bajajauto.com/report/stock_shareholding.html) only serves a shareholding table dated 31 March 2012 with no links to any current filing, its newer IR site (investors.bajajauto.com) has no discoverable shareholding-pattern URL, and a candidate BSE AttachLive PDF surfaced by search returned 404; Bharat Electronics' own site (bel-india.in) fails TLS certificate verification for every request through this environment's proxy (the origin server presents an untrusted certificate chain — confirmed by direct TLS handshake trace, not a proxy-side block) and its WebFetch equivalent 503s. Per this fleet's fallback instruction, the FII/FPI and DII aggregate percentages for these four companies were pulled instead from screener.in (aggregator, tier reported) as of the June 2026 quarter; no individually named foreign holder is recorded for any of the four because screener.in's consolidated view does not disclose named holders, only category aggregates, and the fleet's own reachability notes are explicit that screener.in is 'the fallback of last resort at tier reported' for exactly this reason. This file therefore goes deep on one company (Cipla, documented tier, full Table II/III read) and records the four others honestly as unresourced rather than padding them with unverifiable named-holder guesses. It covers the mandatory comparison set (BlackRock, Vanguard, Norges Bank Investment Management/Government Pension Fund Global, GIC/Government of Singapore, Capital Group, Fidelity, Kuwait Investment Authority, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority) tested against Cipla, and LIC of India as the domestic control (found via a LIC-managed ULIP fund line, not LIC's direct equity book). It leaves out: any claim about the four unverified companies' named foreign holders; Cipla's foreign promoter-family holding (see gaps — persons are never recorded as nodes per CONTRACT rule 1, so the Hamied family's NRI shareholding is described narratively here, not as a claim); adviser mandates and FPI rule-change history, which belong to other files in this domain.

voids.what: Bharat Electronics' own site (bel-india.in) fails TLS certificate verification on every request routed through this environment's proxy: a direct TLS handshake trace shows the proxy tunnel to bel-india.in:443 completes, but the origin server's own certificate is rejected ('unable to get local issuer certificate') even against the full CA bundle — i.e. this is bel-india.in's own certificate chain, not a proxy-side block (the proxy status endpoint confirms bundleCoversEveryHost:true). WebFetch on the same host and on a historic PDF path both returned 503. Per this session's standing instruction never to disable TLS verification, no insecure fetch was used for any data retained in this file.

symmetryCheck: The same lens (open the primary filing, list every named ≥1% foreign holder, name LIC as domestic control) was applied to all five batch-2 companies but could only be executed on one, Cipla, for source-access reasons documented in voids above — not because the other four were skipped. On Cipla, the result matches batch 1's pattern exactly: BlackRock is absent by name (as in all 5 of batch 1's checked companies), Vanguard and NBIM/Government Pension Fund Global each cross 1% via a single named fund line (1.01% and 1.98% respectively), GIC/Capital Group/Fidelity/KIA/ADIA are absent, and LIC's presence is not a clean 'LIC owns X%' figure but a LIC-*managed fund product* line (LICI ASM NON PAR, 6.15%) — the same pattern batch 1 found for LIC in Bharti Airtel (a ULIP fund, not LIC's own book) rather than the clean direct-holding figures batch 1 found for LIC in HDFC Bank, Reliance and ITC. The one asymmetry worth flagging: Cipla's Table II shows a foreign-promoter stake (20.05%, two NRI Hamied-family individuals) that nearly matches every institutional FPI line combined (24.55%) — structurally different from batch 1's BAT/ITC and Suzuki/Maruti foreign-promoter findings in that here the foreign promoter is named individuals, not a corporate/FDI vehicle, which is exactly why CONTRACT rule 1 keeps it out of the claims table even though it is, by percentage, the most consequential foreign ownership fact in this file.

LIC's percentage in Bajaj Auto, Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finserv and Bharat Electronics could not be verified in this pass; a 2022-dated news figure for Bajaj Auto (LIC paring its stake from 7.203% to 5.200%) was found but is too stale to record as a current claim and was discarded rather than presented as current.

Cipla's two NRI/foreign-individual promoters (Yusuf Khwaja Hamied 18.68%, Kamil Hamied 1.35%) are the largest foreign ownership fact in this file by percentage but are excluded from claims under CONTRACT rule 1 (never record persons); a companion 'promoters' or 'persons-in-public-roles' file, if this fleet produces one, is the right place for founder-family promoter shareholding as a distinct question from institutional/passive foreign ownership.
